subject: saban

brief.inclusion: Entertainment and private-equity billionaire who has given more than $40 million in itemized federal contributions, almost all to Democratic committees, and who uses that giving, a Brookings policy center and a Washington forum he funds to press the Democratic Party on Israel.
brief.namesakes: FEC rows for a Haim Saban or Haim Cohen-Saban in Brooklyn (handbag manufacturing, L S Industries) are a different person. The subject files from Los Angeles, Beverly Hills or Burbank with Saban Entertainment, Saban Capital Group or Fox Kids employers. His wife Cheryl Saban gives separately and is not counted.

coverage.lags: FEC Schedule A for the 2026 cycle updates as committees file. California state giving (ballot measures, the 2026 governor and Los Angeles mayor races) is not in the federal record. Saban Capital Group holdings are private.

openQuestions: The "one-issue guy" quotation is attributed to a 2004 New York Times profile; the original wording was not checked.
A 2026 Real Deal report of a gift to Xavier Becerra's California governor campaign could not be opened; state giving needs a California Cal-Access pass.
Confirm the date of the Univision consortium's exit after the 2020–2021 Searchlight sale.
Ethnicity and race: Wikipedia describes an Egyptian-Jewish family; no source states a race directly.

summary: Egyptian-born Israeli-American who made his fortune from Power Rangers and the $5.2 billion sale of Fox Family Worldwide to Disney in 2001, then built Saban Capital Group. He has given more than $40 million in itemized federal contributions since 1988, from a $7 million gift to the Democratic National Committee's building fund in 2002 to $5 million for AIPAC's super PAC, United Democracy Project, since 2022, and he funds the Brookings Middle East center and annual Saban Forum.

chapters.title: Alexandria, Tel Aviv and Paris
chapters.dek: An Egyptian-Jewish refugee who went from rock promoter to children's-television supplier.
chapters.body:
Saban was born in Alexandria, Egypt, on October 15, 1944, to an Egyptian-Jewish family [[wikidata, wikipedia]]. In 1956, after the Suez crisis, the family left for Israel with much of Egypt's Jewish community. He was expelled from a Youth Aliyah boarding school, finished high school at night and served in the Israel Defense Forces [[wikipedia]].

In 1966 he became bassist and manager of a rock band, the Lions of Judah, and went on to promote tours in Israel until losses around the 1973 war left him in debt. He moved to France, where he produced records including the theme for the French version of a Japanese robot cartoon, and in 1983 to the United States, where with Shuki Levy he wrote and supplied music for children's television [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Power Rangers and the Disney sale
chapters.dek: A Japanese-footage franchise and a $5.2 billion exit.
chapters.body:
He founded Saban Entertainment in 1988. Its Mighty Morphin Power Rangers, which spliced Japanese action footage with American actors, became a global franchise in the 1990s [[labj-2026, wikipedia]]. In the mid-1990s he combined his company with News Corporation's children's network in a joint venture that became Fox Family Worldwide [[labj-2026, wikipedia]]. In 1998 ten composers threatened to sue after The Hollywood Reporter reported he had not written all the music credited to him; he settled out of court [[wikipedia]].

In October 2001 Disney completed its purchase of Fox Family Worldwide from Saban and Fox for $5.2 billion, about $2.9 billion in cash plus $2.3 billion in assumed obligations, and renamed the channel ABC Family [[disney-2001]]. Saban's profit was reported at about $1.6 billion [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Saban Capital Group
chapters.dek: German television, Univision and the return of the Power Rangers.
chapters.body:
He founded Saban Capital Group in Century City in 2001 [[labj-2026]]. In 2003 he led a consortium that took control of the German broadcaster ProSiebenSat.1 from the bankrupt Kirch group, and in 2007 sold the stake to KKR and Permira at 22.40 euros a share, three times the 7.5 euros he had paid [[wikipedia]]. The same year a Saban-led consortium completed a $13.7 billion purchase of Univision, the largest Spanish-language broadcaster in the United States; the group agreed in 2020 to sell a majority stake to Searchlight Capital Partners [[forbes-profile, wikipedia]].

He bought the Power Rangers back from Disney in 2010 and sold the franchise and other brands to Hasbro in 2018 for $522 million in cash and stock [[hasbro-2018, forbes-profile]]. He remains chairman and chief executive of Saban Capital Group and sits on the board of Universal Music Group [[labj-2026]]. Forbes estimates his net worth at $3.3 billion and reports that he and his wife have given about $230 million to charity [[forbes-profile]].

chapters.title: Forty million dollars for Democrats
chapters.dek: From party soft money to presidential super PACs to AIPAC's super PAC.
chapters.body:
FEC records show Saban's itemized federal giving beginning in 1988 and growing in the late 1990s, almost all of it to Democrats [[fec-saban]]. The largest entries are from 2002, before the McCain–Feingold ban on party soft money took effect: $7 million to the Democratic National Committee's building fund that January and $3 million more to the party's non-federal account in September [[fec-saban]].

After the 2010 Citizens United decision opened the way for super PACs, his money moved there. He gave $6.1 million to Priorities USA Action, the main pro-Hillary Clinton super PAC, from June 2015 to October 2016, and repeated seven-figure sums to the House and Senate Democratic super PACs from 2014 on [[fec-saban]]. He described his commitment to Clinton's campaign as "eight figures" [[toi-trump-2016]]. He gave to the Biden Victory Fund in 2020 and to the Harris Victory Fund in 2024, and in February 2024 hosted a fundraiser for Biden's reelection that raised $4.5 million [[fec-saban, wrap-rafah-2024]].

Since 2022 his largest recurring gift has gone to United Democracy Project, the super PAC created by AIPAC, which spends in primaries of both parties: $1 million a year from February 2022 to June 2026, $5 million in all [[fec-saban]].

chapters.title: A center at Brookings and a forum of his own
chapters.dek: Buying a seat in the Washington policy debate on the Middle East.
chapters.body:
In May 2002 Brookings announced a Saban Center for Middle East Policy, made possible by his founding grant and directed by Martin Indyk, a former U.S. ambassador to Israel; Saban chaired its international advisory council [[brookings-2002]]. He presented the gift as the act of "someone who has an abiding interest in promoting Arab-Israeli peace" [[brookings-2002]]. The center's grant was reported at about $13 million [[wikipedia]].

The annual Saban Forum, which he funds and Brookings organizes, brings American and Israeli officials together each year [[jta-ellison-2016]]. It is also a platform for Saban's own interventions in Democratic politics.

chapters.title: A Democrat who polices his party on Israel
chapters.dek: Against Trump in 2016, against Ellison at the DNC, for Trump's peace plan, against Biden's weapons pause.
chapters.body:
Saban's best-known description of himself, from a 2004 New York Times interview, is that he is "a one-issue guy, and my issue is Israel" [[nyt-2004]]. In 2016 he campaigned against Donald Trump on Israeli television, calling him a "clown" and "dangerous for Israel" in March and, on the night of Clinton's acceptance speech, "a conman" whose election would be "disastrous" for Israel [[jta-clown-2016, toi-trump-2016]].

That December, at the Saban Forum, he said unprompted that Rep. Keith Ellison, then running to chair the DNC, was "clearly an anti-Semite and anti-Israel individual" and would be "a disaster" for the relationship between Jews and the party. Ellison said the remarks cited against him had been taken out of context [[jta-ellison-2016]].

He parted from his party on specific Trump policies. In January 2020 he endorsed the administration's Middle East plan, crediting Trump and Jared Kushner with "a framework that is out-of-the-box" [[ji-peace-plan-2020]]. That June the UAE's ambassador, Yousef Al Otaiba, enlisted Saban to place an op-ed in Yedioth Ahronoth offering Israel better Arab relations if it dropped plans to annex West Bank land; the Abraham Accords followed that summer [[uae-oped-2020, toi-oped-2021]]. After the January 6 riot he urged Vice President Pence to invoke the 25th Amendment, saying Trump's conduct sounded "like incitement to commit a crime" [[yahoo-25th-2021]].

In May 2024, three months after hosting a Biden fundraiser, he emailed the president's aides Steve Ricchetti and Anita Dunn to protest the pause in bomb shipments to Israel before a Rafah offensive, writing that "Hamas should be defeated" and arguing that more Jewish voters care about Israel than Muslim voters care about Hamas; Muslim American leaders condemned the line [[wrap-rafah-2024, yahoo-rafah-2024]].
